programme: ASCL1, ISL1 and HES6 form a neuroendocrine/proneural lineage-specification module (HES6 is a Notch-pathway antagonist that normally de-represses ASCL1, and ASCL1 targets include HES6's own network node E2F1 and, per the retrieved target lists, ASCL1 itself sits under DNMT3B and DNMT1 regulation); E2F2 and E2F3 form the RB-gated cell-cycle arm that this lineage module runs alongside once RB1 restraint is lost; DNMT1 and DNMT3B are the DNA-methylation machinery that locks the lineage state in and silences classical tumour suppressors.
role_in_a: In lung cancer this is the defining circuitry of neuroendocrine (small-cell) lung cancer: ASCL1 sets neuroendocrine identity and cooperates with ISL1 to mark a distinct, drug-response-relevant subtype, RB1 loss frees E2F3/E2F2 to drive proliferation (documented as a synthetic-lethal dependency), and DNMT3B/DNMT1 methylate downstream loci (e.g. TAL1-PKM2 repression) to entrench the transformed, dedifferentiated state.
role_in_b: In glioma/glioblastoma the record only substantiates two of the seven carrying factors directly: E2F2 sits downstream of PPARα/miR-214 controlling glioma proliferation, and DNMT1 drives glioma proliferation and invasion through NUP37-mediated methylation, with a further paper showing the brain microenvironment itself suppresses DNMT1 in cancer cells resident there. ASCL1, ISL1, HES6 and DNMT3B have no glioma evidence in this material despite being core to normal neural progenitor specification.
shared_axis: Both cancers arise from cells that retain or reactivate a neuroectodermal developmental programme (neuroendocrine epithelium in lung, neuroglial precursors in brain), and both are reported to route proliferation through the same RB-E2F checkpoint release and DNMT1/DNMT3B-mediated methylation; a lineage-specifying module built on ASCL1 with its Notch-buffer HES6 could plausibly operate in glioma by the same general mechanism even without disease-specific documentation here.
reasoning: The module is nameable and coherent from the factors alone, and nearly every carrying factor is well documented in lung cancer specifically, but the cross-disease link is carried by only E2F2 and DNMT1, both through generic cell-cycle/methylation biology rather than anything tying the neuroendocrine lineage arm (ASCL1/ISL1/HES6) to glioma. No paper in the record connects small-cell lung cancer and glioma directly through this axis, and the pairing of a peripheral neuroendocrine epithelial cancer with a primary CNS glial tumour is not an obvious anatomical or clinical link, so the account stands on reasoning about shared developmental biology rather than retrieved fact.
support: PMID 41860961 — RB-loss/E2F3 synthetic lethality ties RB-E2F release to small-cell lung cancer; PMID 42652818 — ASCL1 is part of the neuroendocrine subtyping scheme (with NEUROD1/POU2F3) in lung cancer; PMID 41582485 — ISL1 defines a distinct SCLC neuroendocrine subtype predicting drug response; PMID 41184887 — DNMT3B represses PKM2 transcription via TAL1 in NSCLC, showing methylation-driven reprogramming in lung cancer; PMID 39174498 — NUP37 drives glioma proliferation/invasion through DNMT1-mediated methylation, placing the methylation arm directly in glioma; PMID 32891059 — the brain microenvironment suppresses DNMT1 in resident cancer cells, linking brain tissue context to DNMT1 regulation; PMID 29862267 — PPARα regulates glioma proliferation through miR-214 and E2F2, placing the E2F arm directly in glioma.
how_to_falsify: Perform ASCL1 ChIP-seq/CUT&RUN in glioma or glioblastoma stem-cell lines and test whether ASCL1 binds and regulates the same node genes it controls in SCLC (HES6, ISL1-pathway genes, E2F1); separately, knock down DNMT1/DNMT3B in an RB1-null glioma model and check whether ASCL1 promoter methylation and E2F2/E2F3 activity move together as in lung cancer. If ASCL1 occupancy in glioma does not overlap the SCLC-defined target set, or if DNMT1/DNMT3B methylation state is uncoupled from RB-E2F activity in glioma, the shared-axis account fails.
caveats: All 644 patient-group comparisons come from a single independent cohort pair, so these are subgroup splits of one cohort, not independent replications, and the high concordance fractions (219-251/644) should be read at that scale, not as cross-study reproducibility. The single-view exclusions (ELK1, RFX1, NFX1, etc.) show many other factors were subgroup-specific and rightly dropped, and the tissue-generic exclusions (HDAC7, RFX5, STAT4, EGR4, FOXP3) removed broadly immune/tissue-standard factors, so what remains is closer to a lineage-plasticity/methylation signature than a generic brain-or-lung identity signature. Open Targets records no glioma association for ASCL1, ISL1, HES6, NCOR1, DNMT3B, HBP1, CREB3 or IRF2, consistent with (not proof against) their absence from curated glioma literature; only DNMT1 has clear primary evidence of direct involvement in both diseases in this record.
